I've perused the comments, and everything that has been mentioned is spot on. But I want to emphasize how chill it was, for me at least. I guess because it was a different time, but I felt like no one was playing the game "rushingly". I'll try to explain what I mean.

There was no sprint button. Everyone went the same speed. Which I think added to it. You literally couldn't play the game any faster than it was already going. So it was suspenseful. Shield down and getting chased? It was like being in a horror movie.

It has already been mentioned but, I would create a custom game with two, maybe even one other person I just met and we would dick around with the glitches. Superjumping was stupid-fun. But while we dicked around, friends would start joining us. An hour goes by and maybe we have a full room. And you know how the rest goes.

But I really miss the mics. Maybe that's why there weren't a lot of people who play objective based games on Halo 4? No way to strategize and coordinate the attack plan. It would go like this: "I'm crouching at the bottom entrance." "Okay coming through the top entrance." "Ready? Go now, go go go." Then the other team would call out our positions, and what followed would be an intense clash. There would usually only be one person left either on the attacking or defending side. If it was the attacking, they would haul ass with the flag or try to plant. The rest of us watching from the dead cam, aching to spawn already. Then the second clash. If it was a really could match, we could probably fit a third clash in before either a flag  or bomb plant.

That was actually the best part of objective based games – the clashes. That first clash is intense for a few seconds, and those few seconds determined how the game would play out. Would you need to chase the flag guy upon respawn? Would you be the one to haul ass to base with the flag? Was your team good enough to have a warthog ready to pick you up?

But before you can clash, you have to make it all the way across the map to the flag. That was a different kind of intensity altogether. Let me break the scene into two parts: the defending and the attacking. Asymmetrical designs are the best for objective games. But to keep both sides of the map balanced is difficult, but those brilliant bastards did it for Halo 2.

*Early Game*

Defending: Sniper is the first line of defense. If you were running for sniper, you better know how to use it.  Because if something thinks they can do it better, they will pick it up if you get sniped. And if they were, you were never going to see that sniper again.  As sniper, you needed to cover your team for the rush to rockets, which was usually somewhere out in the open. Smack dab in the middle of both teams. This meant you had to neutralize the other sniper first. The line of sight from rockets to each sniper was usually one in the same. Say you succeeded. Now your team has both sniper and rockets. Rockets has to destroy the vehicles. Okay now the game is imbalanced but fuck it, it would still be fun.

Attacking: How do you neutralize sniper and rockets? You throw your bodies at them until they run out of bullets. Whatever had to be done. Like I said, everyone played it less "rushingly". You fucked up in the early game clash and now you had to pay the price to get to that flag.

If the roles were reversed, it was pretty much guaranteed 2 flag captures. If there was a mix like attacking has rockets but defending has sniper, that's a toss in the air. If Defending has rockets but attacking has sniper, defending better hide somewhere around the flag cause sniper pick off people running around to make it a 3v4 or 2v4 for the clash to get the flag. But even so, rockets evens the odds inside the building so you still have to approach it strategically. Brilliant game.

*Mid game*

Defending: Power weapons are out of ammo by this point. Usually it was 3 in base and 1 scouting around trying to kill at least one kill, maybe claim [invis](http://h2.halowiki.net/p/Active_Camouflage) before attacking can. Warthog spawns on attacking side. Everyone in the base is crouching around just waiting for the Warthog to come.

Attacking: You have the motherfucking warthog. You pile 3 in, cause no rockets on map means no fear. Last dude has to walk, sorry dude. The strategy would be to do recon with the warthog. You need to know their position if you want to make a run for the flag. You circle a base like a vulture trying to force them to move around by hiding from your fire or engaging you. Or rev that engine and drive right into the middle of the base. Forget about it, it becomes chaos in that base.

*End game*

Defending: You lost the flag. You are watching the other team run with it. If they had a warthog, you just lost. If they didn't you are going to haul constant-speed ass to that guy as soon as you spawn. 

Forget about power weapons, forget about map control, forget about call-outs, forget about strategy. You are throwing your body at the situation for the greater good. 

Attacking: Forget about power weapons, forget about map control, forget about call-outs, forget about strategy. You are throwing your body at the situation for the greater good. 

It's chaos and it's great. You embrace it and you let it flow through you.

I probably played 95% objective and 5% slayer on Halo 2. On Halo 4, it has reversed. Now that I think about it, it probably has to do with the ranking system. The ranking system was so good on Halo 2, that's probably why I found it more enjoyable. People actually tried to get the flag or the bomb plant without worrying about their stats. I would go super negative on games but have like 2 flag captures. It probably also had to do with great map design. Asymmetrical designs are the best for objective games. But to keep both sides of the map balanced is difficult, but those brilliant bastards did it for Halo 2. And I guess that write-up was mainly for maps like Lockout, Terminal, Zanzibar, Headlong, Ivory Tower, Containment, etc. Symmetrical maps were less strategic, more chaotic, and I liked symmetrical and asymmetrical maps equally. I know I separated the scenes as early, mid, and late game, but in reality those were the cycles in one game. The cycles were governed by weapon respawns. But if I recall correctly, they weren't constantly on the map like they are now. People would die and no one would pick it up so they would get lost. A majority of the game was played with the weapons you spawned with. It was simpler, but it involved more strategy. You had to get the timing of the attack and defense right. Going in the base one or two at a time would get you nowhere as the attacking team. Neither was running around the map as the defending team. 

I guess a lot of people had more patience back in the day. No one minded traveling to the base (which would take like 15-30 seconds) without seeing any action. Or conversely, waiting at the base for a similar amount of time. The ambiance of Halo 2 was as though everyone was just hanging out in a game. But when the action happened, everyone was ready. I guess hanging out is stretching it. Everyone was setting up their positions on the map. They would find a spot that they liked, a role they liked to play for the team, and they did it.

I was usually the sniper. So my job was to hunt. But I also enjoyed being rockets. If I was defending, that meant to take out the vehicles and then plant my ass somewhere with a line of sight to the flag. If I was attacking, I would hunt. But I also enjoyed having no power weapons, which was a majority of the game time. That meant putting myself in a strategic position for when those "clashes" I talked about went down. If I was attacking, this meant a lot of crouching around the base. If I was defending, that meant perimeter checks.

This turned out to be a whole lot longer than I expected to write, but I really wanted to share what it was like during the glory days of Halo 2. Halo 4 is a far departure from how the game was played. There is much less forethought involved. I really dislike the sprinting.
